passage:
Monday: The history project on the Mughal gardens was due on Friday. Harsha wrote the heading five times on fresh chart paper; each time a letter leaned slightly. Her sister Gargi watched the pile of crumpled sheets grow. "It looks fine!" "It doesn't. It has to be perfect."
Wednesday: Harsha had one good page, then smudged a line and rubbed at it until the paper tore through. She sat on the floor holding the hole up to the light and didn't say anything for a long time.
Friday: The class handed in their projects. Harsha handed in nothing. "I'll bring it Monday, ma'am," she said. At home she told Gargi, "If it's not perfect, it's worse than not giving it." Gargi said, "But nothing gets zero."

qa.q: How many times did Harsha write the heading on Monday?
qa.a: Five times.

qa.q: Why does Harsha feel handing in nothing is better than an imperfect project?
qa.a: Her standard is so high that anything imperfect feels like failing, and she is afraid of being judged, so not submitting seems less painful.

qa.q: What small step could have helped Harsha on Wednesday?
qa.a: Patching the tear or starting the page again with a time limit, and handing in a finished "good enough" version rather than nothing.

qa.q: How does Gargi see the week?
qa.a: Gargi watches the crumpled sheets pile up and thinks the work already looked fine, and is puzzled that nothing is better than something.

grounding: A teenager rewrites a project page until the paper tears and hands in nothing because it is not perfect.

passage: Vijay, you've rewritten that essay four times. Let me tell you about your Nani at fifteen. A teacher once said, "Preeti, your handwriting is the best in the class," and after that every page had to be flawless. If one letter was wrong, I'd tear the whole page out and start again. For my final-year geography record, I redrew the first map eleven times. The eraser went through the paper, twice. The night before submission I had one perfect map and forty empty pages. I didn't submit it. I told the teacher I was ill. I thought a missing record was better than a messy one. It wasn't, beta. It cost me the marks, and nobody ever saw the map. Hand yours in. Messy is finished.

qa.q: How many times did young Preeti redraw the first map?
qa.a: Eleven times.

qa.q: Why did young Preeti think a missing record was better than a messy one?
qa.a: After the teacher's praise, anything less than flawless felt like losing that identity, so not submitting seemed safer than showing imperfect work.

qa.q: What choice does Nani urge Vijay to make?
qa.a: To hand the essay in now, even messy, because finishing matters more than a perfect page nobody sees.

qa.q: What might Vijay feel hearing that Nani did the same thing?
qa.a: Vijay may feel understood and less ashamed of the rewriting, and more willing to stop, since Nani knows exactly where it leads.

grounding: A grandmother recalls redrawing a map until the paper tore at fifteen and handing in nothing.

passage: The drawing exam gave each Class 11 student one sheet of cartridge paper and two hours. Jomon began a still life of a jug and three onions. The jug's curve looked wrong. He erased it. Drew it again. Erased. By the end of the first hour the paper had gone grey and fuzzy where the jug should be. Avni, at the next easel, had finished her outline and started shading. Jomon pressed harder with the eraser, and the sheet ripped in a jagged line. There was no second sheet. He stared at the tear, then quietly put his pencils away. When the invigilator collected the papers, his was blank except for the torn grey patch. Outside, Avni asked what happened. "It wasn't good enough," he said. "Nothing would've been good enough."

qa.q: What was Jomon drawing?
qa.a: A still life of a jug and three onions.

qa.q: What does "Nothing would've been good enough" reveal about Jomon's mind?
qa.a: He felt defeated, because his standard was so high that no drawing could meet it, so stopping felt less painful than finishing something he'd judge a failure.

qa.q: What could Jomon try in the next timed exam?
qa.a: Allow the first outline to stand, move on to the onions and shading, and fix only at the end, so a whole drawing gets finished.

qa.q: How might Avni feel seeing Jomon's torn blank sheet?
qa.a: Avni may feel shocked and sad, having watched a capable classmate erase his way to nothing while she moved on to shading.

grounding: Under exam time pressure, a teenager erases a drawing until the paper tears and submits nothing.

passage: In their Chennai flat, Keerthana had been on the first page of her English essay since seven. The opening line was never right. She wrote it, read it, rubbed it out. Wrote it again. By ten the top of the paper had worn thin and grey, and when she pressed the eraser once more, it tore. Her younger brother Sahil peeped in. "Akka, it's due tomorrow. Just write the rest." "I can't write the rest if the start is wrong." "Your last essay got 18 out of 20." "That's why this one can't be worse." She took a fresh sheet. The clock ticked past eleven. In the morning she handed in nothing and told the teacher she'd left it at home. It felt safer than a page that wasn't perfect.

qa.q: What happened when Keerthana pressed the eraser once more?
qa.a: The paper tore.

qa.q: Why did handing in nothing feel safer to Keerthana?
qa.a: With the bar set at her last 18 or better, any imperfect page felt like failing, so not finishing avoided being judged.

qa.q: What small step could Keerthana try next time the opening won't come right?
qa.a: Leave a rough first line and write the rest, then come back to it; a messy draft that exists can be improved, but a blank page can't.

qa.q: How might Sahil feel watching his sister erase until the paper tore?
qa.a: Sahil might be puzzled and worried, seeing that the problem isn't ability, since her last essay got 18, but a fear he can't talk her out of.

grounding: A teenager rewrites the opening of an essay until the paper tears and hands in nothing because finishing imperfectly feels like failing.

passage:
"Urmila, why is the bin full of chart paper?"
"It's the science poster, Papa. It keeps going wrong."
Her father, Darshan, pulled out a sheet. "This looks good. What's wrong with it?"
"The title's not centred. And on the next one the arrow's crooked."
"How many sheets have you used?"
"Seven."
"When is it due?"
"Tomorrow." Her voice cracked. "If it isn't perfect, it's not worth giving. Ma'am will put it on the wall with everyone else's."
Darshan sat on the floor beside her. "So right now you have zero posters and seven nearly good ones."
"Nearly isn't good."
"Pick the least-bad one. Finish it in one hour, crooked arrow and all. Then dinner."
Urmila stared at the pile. "What if it's ugly?"
"Then it's a finished ugly poster. That beats an empty space on the wall."

qa.q: How many sheets had Urmila used?
qa.a: Seven.

qa.q: What does 'Nearly isn't good' show about Urmila's thinking?
qa.a: Urmila feels anxious and upset, her voice cracking, because anything short of perfect counts as failure to her, so a flawed poster on the wall seems worse than none.

qa.q: What choice does Darshan suggest, and why could it help?
qa.a: Picking the least-bad sheet and finishing it within an hour; a time limit and permission to be imperfect turn endless redoing into something handed in.

qa.q: How might Darshan feel seeing seven good-looking sheets in the bin?
qa.a: Darshan is probably surprised and concerned, since the work looks good to him, and realises the problem is her fear of imperfection, not her skill.

grounding: A teenager restarts a poster seven times because none is perfect and risks handing in nothing, until her father sets a limit.

passage:
A Tuesday in August. Vishal sat at his desk with the history project page. The first sentence looked clumsy. He erased it. The second try was worse. By midnight the paper had a grey smudge in the middle and a small tear. He threw it away and started a new sheet.

The Friday after. Still no page to show. His sister Zeenat found a pile of torn sheets under his bed. "Vishal, this is the fourth page. Why not just finish one?" "Because it isn't good enough." "Good enough for what?" He didn't answer. He didn't know.

The next Monday. The deadline came. Vishal handed in nothing. His teacher said, "Zero, then." At home, he stared at the torn sheets. "Even a clumsy page would've been better than nothing," he muttered. It felt like a stone in his stomach.

qa.q: How many pages had Vishal torn by Friday?
qa.a: Four pages.

qa.q: Why did finishing a page feel impossible to Vishal?
qa.a: He felt nothing he wrote was good enough, so finishing a clumsy page felt like failing, and he felt stuck and anxious.

qa.q: What could Vishal try next time?
qa.a: He could set a small goal, like finishing a rough draft first, then improving it, instead of aiming for perfect in one go.

qa.q: How might Zeenat feel finding the torn pages?
qa.a: Zeenat seems puzzled and worried, seeing her brother struggle but not understanding why.

grounding: It shows a teenager who keeps erasing and rewriting until he hands in nothing, because finishing feels like failing, over several days.

passage: Zubin, you think I was always relaxed about work? Sit. In Class 10, in Surat, I had to write an essay for the inter-school competition. I wrote the first paragraph fourteen times. Every time, a word felt wrong, and I rubbed it out. The rubber went through the paper. I cried. My mother said, "Parveen, beti, send what you have." I couldn't. What I had wasn't perfect. The deadline passed. A girl from my class, who wrote hers in one evening, won third prize. I was angry at her, but I was angrier at myself. That night I understood something. My essay wasn't bad. It just didn't exist. Now, when I see you rewriting your science notes for the third time, I want to tell you: finished beats perfect.

qa.q: How many times did Parveen write the first paragraph?
qa.a: Fourteen times.

qa.q: How did young Parveen feel when the rubber went through the paper?
qa.a: She felt upset and helpless, crying because nothing felt perfect enough to send.

qa.q: What turning point in the story could have changed the result for young Parveen?
qa.a: If Parveen had followed the mother's advice to send what she had, the essay would have existed and been judged, instead of missing the deadline.

qa.q: How might Parveen's mother have felt watching her daughter cry over the essay?
qa.a: Her mother likely felt sad and worried, wanting Parveen to see that a finished essay was better than none.

grounding: It shows an elder recalling how, as a teenager, she rewrote the same page until it tore and missed the deadline because finishing felt like failing.

passage: The school's creative writing contest had a strict rule: forty-five minutes, one story, handwritten. Charu sat in the exam hall with the fan clattering overhead. She wrote the opening line. Crossed it out. Wrote it again. Rubbed out a word so hard the paper thinned. The invigilator called, "Twenty minutes left." Charu had three lines and a hole in the page. Across the aisle, her friend Hrithik was writing steadily, not stopping to fix anything. Charu tore off the page and started again. "Ten minutes." Four lines. Her heart was pounding. When the bell rang, she handed in a sheet with a title and half a paragraph. Outside, Hrithik said, "Mine's a mess, but it's done." Charu felt tears prick her eyes. His mess would be read. Her perfect first line wouldn't.

qa.q: How long did the contest allow for the story?
qa.a: Forty-five minutes.

qa.q: Why did Charu keep erasing and restarting?
qa.a: She felt anxious that nothing was good enough, so each flaw seemed unbearable and finishing a messy story felt like failing.

qa.q: What could Charu try next time the clock is running?
qa.a: She could write the whole story roughly first, then fix only a few lines at the end, so there is something finished to hand in.

qa.q: How does Hrithik see his own messy story?
qa.a: Hrithik seems relaxed, accepting that it's messy but proud it's done, which contrasts with Charu's fear.

grounding: It shows a teenager who rewrites the same page because it isn't perfect and ends up handing in almost nothing, as finishing feels like failing.

passage:
Kiran, sixteen, had been rewriting the first page of her history essay since six o'clock. By ten, the rubber had worn a hole in the paper.
Her friend Amandeep, studying on video call, said, “Just finish it. It's due tomorrow.”
“It's not right yet. The first line is boring.”
“It's fine!”
“It's not fine. If it's not perfect, it's not worth handing in.”
She tore the page out and started again. Same first line, slightly different. Erased it again.
At midnight she had a pile of crumpled pages and no essay.
The next morning she told the teacher she'd forgotten it at home. It was easier than handing in something imperfect. On the bus she felt sick. She had done nothing, and somehow that felt safer than doing something okay.

qa.q: How long had Kiran been rewriting the first page by ten?
qa.a: She had been rewriting it since six o'clock, four hours.

qa.q: Why did Kiran keep erasing the first line?
qa.a: She felt anxious that it had to be perfect, and handing in something imperfect felt like failing.

qa.q: What could Kiran try next time?
qa.a: Write a rough draft all the way to the end first, then improve it, so finishing isn't blocked by a perfect first line.

qa.q: How might Amandeep feel watching Kiran start again?
qa.a: Amandeep probably feels frustrated and worried, seeing a friend stuck on one line.

grounding: The passage shows a teenager rewriting the same page until the paper tears and handing in nothing, because finishing feels like failing.

passage:
“Vidya, it's eleven. Are you still on the same drawing?”
“It's not right, Shankar Bhaiya.”
“It looked fine at eight.”
“The shading's wrong. I erased it.”
“Again?”
“The paper's torn now.” Her voice cracked. “I'll have to start from the beginning.”
“It's due tomorrow.”
“I know! But if it's not perfect, I can't hand it in.”
“Can I see?”
She held it up. There was a hole where the tree's shadow had been.
“Vidya, it was a good drawing. Honestly. Better than anything I could do.”
“Good isn't enough.”
Shankar sat on her bed. “You know what happens if you hand in nothing?”
“I get zero.”
“And if you hand in the one from eight o'clock?”
Vidya went quiet. She looked at the torn paper for a long time.

qa.q: What had Vidya erased too many times?
qa.a: She had erased the shading until the paper tore.

qa.q: How did Vidya feel when her voice cracked?
qa.a: She felt upset and trapped, believing anything less than perfect would count as failure.

qa.q: What point did Shankar make that could help Vidya?
qa.a: That handing in a good drawing is better than handing in nothing, since a zero is the real failure.

qa.q: How does Shankar see Vidya's drawing?
qa.a: Shankar thinks it was good, better than he could do, and is worried to see her so upset.

grounding: The dialogue shows a teenager erasing a drawing until the paper tears because it isn't perfect, so finishing feels like failing.

passage:
My Class 10 science project was due on a Monday. I'm Ishita, and I didn't hand it in.
It wasn't laziness. I'd started a week before. I wrote the introduction, then decided it was clumsy, and rewrote it. Then again. By Friday I had seventeen versions of one paragraph and my eraser had gone through the page twice. The rest of the project didn't exist.
My friend Dolma kept saying, “Just write the rest, you can fix it later.” But I couldn't move past something that wasn't perfect. It felt like building a house on a crack.
On Monday I told the teacher I was ill. I wasn't. I just couldn't hand in something I thought was bad.
I got a zero. The thing I was so afraid of, a bad mark, happened anyway, only worse. That's when I started to see the trap.

qa.q: How many versions of the introduction did Ishita write?
qa.a: Ishita wrote seventeen versions of one paragraph.

qa.q: Why couldn't Ishita move past the introduction?
qa.a: Ishita felt anxious that anything imperfect would be failure, so finishing felt impossible.

qa.q: What did Dolma suggest, and why is it a good strategy?
qa.a: To write the rest and fix it later, because a finished rough draft can be improved, while a perfect paragraph alone gets nothing.

qa.q: How might Dolma have felt when Ishita got a zero?
qa.a: Dolma probably felt sad and frustrated, having tried to help a friend finish.

grounding: The reflection shows a teenager rewriting the same paragraph so often that nothing is handed in, because the standard makes finishing feel like failing.

passage:
English teacher's note, Class 10-B — Payal
Jeevan did not submit his essay on Monday. When I asked, he showed me his notebook. The first page had been written, rubbed out and rewritten so many times that the paper had torn through in two places.
He said he had started the introduction nine times. "It wasn't good enough, ma'am. The first sentence has to be perfect or the whole essay is bad." He looked exhausted, and his hands were grey with eraser dust.
He is one of my strongest writers. I think he has set the bar so high that completing anything feels like losing.
I told him that a finished, imperfect draft gets more from me than a perfect sentence that never arrives. I asked for a rough draft by Wednesday, in pen, no erasing allowed, and promised feedback, not a grade.
He brought it on Wednesday. It was good.

qa.q: How many times had Jeevan started the introduction?
qa.a: He had started it nine times.

qa.q: Why does Jeevan keep rewriting the first page?
qa.a: He feels anxious that anything less than a perfect first sentence will ruin the essay, so finishing feels like failing to him.

qa.q: Why was the teacher's request for a rough draft in pen a good idea?
qa.a: It removed the chance to erase endlessly and took away the grade pressure, so Jeevan could finish something and get feedback.

qa.q: How might the teacher see Jeevan's Wednesday draft?
qa.a: The teacher sees it as good, and as proof that a finished imperfect draft is worth far more than a perfect first sentence that never arrives.

grounding: It shows, through a teacher's note, a teenager rewriting the same page until it tears and handing in nothing, because his standard makes finishing feel like failing.

passage:
Thursday, 11:40 p.m.
The biology project is due tomorrow and I have nothing. Not because I didn't work. I, Alka, worked for five hours tonight.
I drew the heart diagram. The left ventricle was slightly too big, so I erased it. Drew it again. The labels were crooked. Erased. By the sixth try the paper went fuzzy, and on the seventh it tore right through the aorta.
I started a new sheet. Same thing. Now there are four torn sheets in the bin and a blank one on the desk.
Maria finished hers in an hour. It's messy, and she's happy. I looked at hers and thought, I'd rather hand in nothing than hand in that.
But that means I'm handing in nothing. How is nothing better than messy? I don't know. It just feels like if it's not perfect, it's proof I'm bad at it.

qa.q: How many hours did Alka work on the project tonight?
qa.a: Alka worked for five hours tonight.

qa.q: How does Alka feel at 11:40 p.m.?
qa.a: Alka feels frustrated and stuck, knowing nothing is finished and that an imperfect diagram would feel like proof of being bad at biology.

qa.q: What could Alka try before the deadline?
qa.a: Alka could set a timer, draw the diagram once in pen without erasing, and hand it in, treating a finished, messy version as better than nothing.

qa.q: How does Maria seem to see her own project?
qa.a: Maria is happy with a messy but finished project, which shows she sees finishing as the goal, not perfection.

grounding: It shows a teenager redrawing the same diagram until the paper tears and ending up with nothing, because the standard makes finishing feel like failing.

passage:
Winter fog lay over the fields outside the kasba school, and the classroom windows were grey by four. The history notebook was due tomorrow.
Eshaan had begun his answer on the Mauryan empire nine times. Each time a letter leaned the wrong way, or a line ran crooked, he rubbed it out. The paper had gone thin and grey in the middle.
"Just write it, yaar," Sarika said from the next bench. "Sir only checks if it's there."
"It has to be right." He pressed the eraser again and the page split with a soft rip. He stared at the hole.
The next day, when Sir collected notebooks, Eshaan's page was empty except for the torn patch. He said he had forgotten it at home. It felt easier than handing in something he'd have hated.

qa.q: How many times had Eshaan begun his answer on the Mauryan empire?
qa.a: He had begun it nine times.

qa.q: Why does Eshaan say he forgot the notebook instead of handing in what he had?
qa.a: He feels ashamed and stuck, because anything less than perfect feels like failing, so handing in nothing seems less painful.

qa.q: What small step could help Eshaan next time?
qa.a: He could set a rule to write a full rough draft without erasing, then fix only one or two things before handing it in.

qa.q: If you were Sarika, what would you want Eshaan to know?
qa.a: Sarika would probably want him to know that a messy, finished answer is better than an empty page, and that watching him tear it was worrying.

grounding: A teenager erases and rewrites until the page tears and hands in nothing, because an imperfect answer feels like failure.
